_meta: Two hues on the color wheel and the number of steps of a gradient between them, used to show why interpolating hue must follow the shorter arc around the circle, not a straight linear interpolation of the two angle numbers. Hue is an angle in [0, 360): 0 and 360 are the same red, so the color wheel wraps at that seam. A gradient from one hue to another should sweep along the shorter of the two arcs between them. Linear interpolation of the raw angles -- start + t*(end - start) -- ignores the wrap: when the two hues straddle the seam (for example 350 and 20, which are only 30 degrees apart going through red), the raw difference end - start is 20 - 350 = -330, so the naive interpolation sweeps 330 degrees the long way around, straight through cyan and green -- the opposite side of the wheel -- and its midpoint lands near the color complementary to both endpoints instead of between them. The fix is to compute the signed shortest angular difference: if end - start is greater than 180 or less than -180, add or subtract 360 so the step is at most 180 degrees, interpolate along that shorter arc, and wrap the result back into [0, 360). On this fixture the two hues are 350 (red) and 20 (a warm red-orange), 30 degrees apart the short way; the naive interpolation passes through cyan (midpoint about 185) while the shortest-arc interpolation stays in the reds (midpoint about 5). start_hue and end_hue are the endpoint hues in degrees; steps is how many samples of the gradient to produce (including both endpoints). These are the fixture; the two interpolated sweeps, the arc lengths, and the midpoints are computed.
